etymology: Hebrew Dinhabah, perhaps “place of plunder” or “giving of judgment”; the royal city of Bela the son of Beor, first-named king of Edom.
biblical_def: Before ever a king reigned over the children of Israel, Bela the son of Beor sat enthroned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah: “And Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom: and the name of his city was Dinhabah” (Gen 36:32). The chronicler marks the order plainly — these “reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel” (1Ch 1:43). Here is a parable of the two seeds. Esau was the elder, and Esau's line came early to crowns and cities while Jacob's sons yet groaned in Egypt and wandered without a throne. The kingdoms of men flourish first; the kingdom of God tarries, for it is not of this order. Edom had her Dinhabah, her walls and her monarch, while the promise slept in the loins of a servant people. Yet the LORD had said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” and Malachi seals it: “I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau.” Election runs not by birthright nor by the swiftness of earthly greatness. Dinhabah rose betimes and is fallen; its very site is lost, a name in the genealogy of the reprobate line. But the throne given to David and to David's greater Son endures for ever. Let no saint envy the early crowns of Edom; the kingdom that comes slowly comes to stay.
webster_summary: The royal city of Bela, first king of Edom, who reigned before any king reigned in Israel (Gen 36:32); a witness that the kingdoms of men rise early and pass, while the kingdom of God endures.

etymology: Hebrew 'Avith, perhaps “ruins” or “overturning”; the royal city of Hadad son of Bedad, king of Edom, who smote Midian in the field of Moab.
biblical_def: The roll of Edom's kings turns like a passing bell: one reigns, one dies, another rises in his stead. Of Avith we read, “And Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Avith” (Gen 36:35). Here was a warrior-king, a man of the sword who smote Midian in the open field and made his name in blood. The might of Esau's line was no fable; Edom bred dukes and captains and mighty men, and the field of Moab felt the weight of Hadad's arm. Yet mark how the record closes upon him — he smites, he reigns, he dies, and Samlah rises after. Earthly conquest without the covenant is a candle that burns bright and gutters out. The strength of the flesh wins its field and cannot keep its own life. Avith is named once and never again; the city of a conqueror becomes a footnote in the ledger of the reprobate line. So passes the glory of the world. The children of promise are not called to smite Midian in the field, but to overcome by the blood of the Lamb; and their King, who was slain, dieth no more. The mighty of Edom fell each in his turn; the meek inherit the earth, and their inheritance fadeth not away.

etymology: Hebrew Pa'u (also Pai), perhaps “bleating” or “crying out”; the royal city of Hadar, the last-named king of Edom in Genesis.
biblical_def: At the end of the Genesis list stands Hadar, and the name of his city was Pau: “And Baalhanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Pau; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab” (Gen 36:39). He is the last of the eight, and the Spirit lingers only over his wife and her line, as if to say the dynasty had nothing left to boast but a marriage. So ends a kingdom. Man's kingdoms run their appointed course and are written off in half a verse; the throne that seemed everlasting is closed with a name and a genealogy of women. Where is Pau? None can point to it. The kings of Edom reigned and died and were forgotten, for they were the pomp of a people the LORD had set beside the elect line, not within it. But the seed of promise endures. When Edom's list was sealed, the true King was not yet come; and when He came, born of a woman, of the house of David, His kingdom knew no last name in the roll, for of the increase of His government and peace there shall be no end. Pau preaches the mortality of every crown that is not Christ's, and the everlasting stability of the throne that is.

etymology: Hebrew Masreqah, from a root soreq for the choice vine, hence “place of the noble vine” or “vineyard”; the home city of Samlah, king of Edom.
biblical_def: Masrekah is a name we should never have known but that the Spirit of God saw fit to write it: “And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:36). A single verse, a single king, a city otherwise lost to all memory — and yet the Holy Ghost recorded it. Why should the inspired page trouble itself with the petty thrones of Edom, the reprobate line of Esau? Because the God who chose Jacob is sovereign over Esau also. He numbers the kings of the cast-away no less than the kings of the covenant; not a duke of Edom rises but by His decree, not one dies but in His appointed hour. The doctrine of election is no mere favoritism; it is the rule of the Most High over both vessels, the vessel of mercy and the vessel of wrath. Samlah of Masrekah reigned because God ordained his little day, and passed because God had numbered it. Herein is comfort: the same hand that governs the throne of the wicked upholds the least of His saints. If the LORD keeps a book of Edom's forgotten kings, how much more are the names of His people graven in the Lamb's book of life. Masrekah, the place of the choice vine, reminds us that nothing is too small for providence, and no crown too great to escape it.
webster_summary: The home city of Samlah, king of Edom (Gen 36:36); a witness that God is sovereign over the reprobate line of Esau as well as the elect line of Jacob.

etymology: Hebrew Rechoboth ha-Nahar, “broad places by the river”; from rachab, to be wide; the city of Saul (Shaul), king of Edom.
biblical_def: Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in Edom: “And Samlah died, and Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:37). The name Rehoboth means broad places, room, wide streets — a city of spacious ways set beside a river. It sounds like blessing, like the enlargement Isaac once named when the LORD made room for him and he was fruitful in the land. But this Rehoboth belonged to Edom, and its breadth was for a season only. The LORD maketh room for whom He will; He set the bounds of the nations and gave to Esau the mount of Seir for a possession. Yet room granted to the reprobate line is not the everlasting inheritance. Edom had her broad places and her river-city, and where are they now? The streets are silence, the kingdom a list of dead kings. The saint learns here to weigh what breadth is worth the having. There is a room the world gives, wide and pleasant for a day; and there is the place the Lord prepares, “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16). Better a narrow gate that opens on the city of God than all the broad ways of Edom. The LORD who setteth thy foot in a large place hath set thee there for glory, not for a passing reign beside a fading river.

etymology: Hebrew 'Uts, a land of the east reckoned toward Edom; the country where Job dwelt, perhaps named from Uz the son of Aram or of Dishan the Horite.
biblical_def: Away in the land of Uz, in the country of the east reckoned toward Edom, the LORD had a worshipper: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1). It is a wonder of sovereign grace that in the borders of Esau's kin, outside the covenant nation, God kept a man who feared Him and turned from evil. Grace is not bound to a bloodline; the wind bloweth where it listeth. Lamentations sets Uz within Edom's shadow: “O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz” (Lam 4:21). Yet in that land lived the pattern of tried and vindicated faith. Job was brought into the school of affliction, stripped of children, goods, and health, sifted by Satan yet hedged by God, that his faith might be proved and the accuser silenced. He is the great type of the sufferer who holds fast: “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” And the LORD justified His servant, restored him double, and vindicated the way of trust before all the comforters. The land of Uz teaches that God has His hidden ones in unlikely places, that affliction is His refining fire, and that tried faith shall be openly owned by the God who ordained the trial.

etymology: Hebrew Ramath ha-Mitspeh, “the height of the watchtower”; from ramah, height, and mitspeh, a lookout or place of watching; a border town of Gad in Gilead.
biblical_def: On the border of Gad, in the hill-country of Gilead, stood Ramath-mizpeh, the height of the watchtower: “And from Heshbon unto Ramathmizpeh, and Betonim; and from Mahanaim unto the border of Debir” (Josh 13:26). The name joins ramah, a height, with mizpah, a watchtower or place of watching — a lofty lookout set at the frontier of the inheritance. It carries the memory of that older Mizpah where Jacob and Laban reared their heap and said, “The LORD watch between me and thee.” So this height on Gad's edge preaches the God who keeps watch over the borders of His people. The tribes east of Jordan lay exposed to the nations; their frontier needed a watchtower. And is not the whole pilgrim life lived at the border, where the world presses hard against the promise? The saint dwells at the frontier and must watch and pray, for the enemy prowls at the marches of the soul. Yet the true Watchman never slumbers: “so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever” (Psa 125:2). Ramath-mizpeh calls us to lift our eyes unto the hills, whence cometh our help, and to trust the eye that never closes upon the flock. Vigilance is ours; the keeping is the LORD's, who set the tower and mans it Himself.

etymology: Hebrew Neballat, of uncertain sense, perhaps “hidden folly” or a personal name; a town of Benjamin resettled after the return from Babylon.
biblical_def: When the captivity was ended and the remnant came home, they returned not to an empty map but to towns rebuilt and repeopled, and among them Neballat: “Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat” (Neh 11:34). A bare name in a list of resettlement, yet full of mercy. Benjamin, the little tribe, spread again into her villages after the long exile in Babylon; the LORD was replanting His people town by town. Here is grace after chastening. He had scattered them for their sins, given them into the hand of the king of Babylon, and made the land keep her sabbaths in desolation. But the God who wounds also binds; the same faithfulness that sent them into exile brought them home by the decree of Cyrus, according to the word of Jeremiah. Not a tribe was lost, not a promise failed; He set them again in Hadid and Zeboim and Neballat, small places made glad by the return. So the LORD deals with His own: the rod for a season, then the restoring hand. And this replanting in the land was but a shadow of the greater ingathering, when He shall gather His elect from the four winds and settle them in the city that hath foundations. Neballat, obscure and dear, testifies that God forgets none of His people, and after chastening plants them where they shall no more be plucked up.

Neballat was one of the towns of the resettlement.
Its name testifies to grace after chastening.

etymology: Hebrew Yizre'el, “God soweth”; the city in the plain of Esdraelon where Ahab kept a palace, distinct from the valley that bears its name.
biblical_def: In the plain of Esdraelon stood the city of Jezreel, where Ahab kept a palace and Naboth kept a vineyard: “Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria” (1Ki 21:1). The name means God soweth, and God sowed there a harvest of judgment. Ahab coveted, Jezebel murdered, and the innocent blood cried from the ground. Then came the word of the LORD: “The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel” (1Ki 21:23). Years passed and the wicked seemed to prosper, but the word did not fall to the ground. In the appointed day Jehu drove furiously, Jezebel was cast down from her window, and the dogs ate her flesh by that same wall, so that they found no more of her than the skull and the feet: “This is the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Elijah” (2Ki 9:36). Here is the certainty of prophecy and the surety of vengeance. God is not mocked; the blood of the innocent is required, and every idle boast of the tyrant is answered in its hour. Jezreel, distinct from the wide valley that bears its name, preaches that the LORD soweth judgment as surely as mercy, and reapeth in exact fulfilment. The mills of God grind slow, but they grind to the very letter of His word.
webster_summary: The city of Ahab's palace and Naboth's vineyard, where the dogs ate Jezebel by the wall as the LORD had spoken (1Ki 21:1); a witness to the certainty of the prophetic word and the avenging of innocent blood.
webster_full: JEZREEL, the city of Ahab's palace, distinct from the valley of the name.
The name means “God soweth” (from Yizre'el).
There Naboth was murdered for his vineyard (1Ki 21:1).
There the dogs ate Jezebel by the wall, as Elijah foretold (2Ki 9:36).
A witness that God soweth judgment as surely as He soweth mercy.
scriptures: And it came to pass after these things, that Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.
And of Jezebel also spake the LORD, saying, The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.

Wherefore they came again, and told him. And he said, This is the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Elijah the Tishbite, saying, In the portion of Jezreel shall dogs eat the flesh of Jezebel:

And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
corruption_summary: The city of Ahab's crime and Jezebel's doom; it recovers the certainty of the prophetic word and the avenging of innocent blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The story of Naboth is a genuine and timeless rebuke to the abuse of power, but it needs no modern reframing. Scripture itself names the sin plainly: covetousness, false witness, and murder cloaked in a fast and a form of law.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of God's word and the surety of His vengeance. Years passed and Jezebel seemed secure, yet the dogs ate her by the very wall Elijah had named. God is not mocked; the blood of the innocent is required. He soweth judgment as surely as mercy, and reapeth to the very letter of His word.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yizre'el, from zara' (to sow) and El (God); “God soweth,” the name of the city and the plain.
roots_lines: Jezreel — “God soweth,” the city of Ahab's palace (1Ki 21:1).
From zara', to sow, and El, God.
The name signifies both fruitful sowing and the sowing of judgment.
The city is distinct from the broad valley or plain of Jezreel.
Hosea used the name prophetically of both scattering and gathering.
usage: Naboth had a vineyard in Jezreel, hard by Ahab's palace.
The dogs ate Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
Jezreel means God soweth, and He sowed there a harvest of judgment.

etymology: Hebrew Hor ha-Har, “Hor the mountain”; a height marking the ideal north border of the land toward the entrance of Hamath, distinct from the Hor where Aaron died.
biblical_def: When the LORD drew the borders of the promised land, He set a Mount Hor for the northern march — not the Hor where Aaron died in the south, but another height toward the entering in of Hamath: “And this shall be your north border: from the great sea ye shall point out for you mount Hor” (Num 34:7); “from mount Hor ye shall point out your border unto the entrance of Hamath” (Num 34:8). It is a solemn thing that God Himself surveyed the inheritance, staking every corner and naming every landmark of the gift. The bounds of His people are not left to chance nor to the sword of man; the Most High divideth to the nations their inheritance and appointeth the borders of His own. Israel never possessed the whole in her unbelief, falling short of the fulness the LORD had marked. Yet the appointed measure stands; what God bounded, God will bestow. This northern Hor points beyond Canaan to the true and heavenly country, whose dimensions the Lamb hath measured and whose bounds no unbelief shall shrink. There the inheritance is entered in full, incorruptible and undefiled, reserved for the heirs of promise. Mount Hor of the north teaches us to measure our hope by God's appointment and not by our attainment; the land He drew for His people they shall wholly inherit in the resurrection, when the borders of glory are entered without loss.
webster_summary: A height marking the ideal north border of the land toward the entrance of Hamath (Num 34:7), distinct from the Hor where Aaron died; a witness that God appoints the bounds of the inheritance, awaited in full in the heavenly Canaan.
webster_full: MOUNT HOR of the north, a marker of the land's ideal upper border.
“This shall be your north border…ye shall point out for you mount Hor” (Num 34:7).
From it the border ran to the entrance of Hamath (Num 34:8).
A different Hor from the southern mount where Aaron died.
A figure of the full inheritance measured by God, entered in glory.
scriptures: And this shall be your north border: from the great sea ye shall point out for you mount Hor:
From mount Hor ye shall point out your border unto the entrance of Hamath; and the goings forth of the border shall be to Zedad:
And the border shall go on to Ziphron, and the goings out of it shall be at Hazarenan: this shall be your north border.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: The northern Mount Hor of the land's ideal border; it recovers the truth that God appoints the bounds of the inheritance, entered in full only in the heavenly Canaan.
corruption_paragraphs: A border landmark named twice raises no live modern quarrel. Its value is that the LORD Himself surveyed the inheritance, so that the bounds of His people rest on His appointment and not on the shifting sword of man.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the fulness of the inheritance. Israel in unbelief never possessed the whole He had marked, yet the appointed measure stands. What God bounded He will bestow; the northern Hor points to the heavenly country, entered in full and without loss by the heirs of promise.
roots_summary: Hebrew Hor, a mountain or height (a doubled form, “Hor the mountain”); here the northern border-marker of the land.
roots_lines: Mount Hor (north) — a marker of the land's ideal upper border (Num 34:7).
Hor is simply “mountain” or “height.”
The border ran from it to the entrance of Hamath and Zedad.
Distinct from the southern Mount Hor where Aaron died (Num 20).
Located toward Lebanon in the far north of the promised bounds.
usage: The north border was to be pointed out from mount Hor.
